ai.definition: Space-Based Solar Power (SBDSP) involves deploying large-scale solar arrays in orbit around Earth to capture sunlight continuously without atmospheric interference, then transmitting this energy back to Earth for use.
ai.howItWorks: Solar panels on the space-based array convert sunlight into electricity. This electrical power is then transmitted wirelessly via microwaves or lasers to a receiving station on Earth's surface. The received energy is converted back into usable electricity and distributed through existing grid infrastructure.
ai.problemSolved: Overcoming limitations of ground-based solar power, such as intermittent output due to weather conditions and night-time darkness, by providing consistent, uninterrupted solar energy collection in space.
ai.manufacturing: Requires advanced materials science for lightweight yet durable solar panels and robust transmission equipment. Manufacturing involves complex assembly processes that must withstand the harsh conditions of space.
ai.buildProcess: Involves launching components into orbit using heavy-lift rockets, assembling them in space, and establishing a ground receiving station. This process is highly complex and currently beyond current technological capabilities and economic feasibility.
ai.costDrivers: High initial development costs, launch costs for materials, assembly in space, and the need for advanced technologies that are not yet commercially available or economically viable.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is still in its nascent stages with significant technical and economic challenges. However, it has potential to become a major renewable energy source if these issues can be resolved.
ai.regulation: Currently lacks specific regulatory frameworks as the technology is not yet deployed at scale. Regulatory bodies are likely to develop guidelines for space-based operations and environmental impact assessments.
ai.risks: Technological feasibility, economic viability, launch and maintenance costs, risk of space debris, potential geopolitical implications, and environmental concerns during deployment and decommissioning.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current technological and economic limitations. Potential profitability could increase if the technology becomes more efficient or if there is a significant shift towards renewable energy sources.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on reducing costs through advancements in materials science, propulsion technologies for space launches, and improvements in wireless power transmission methods.

glossary.def: A technology involving the deployment of large-scale solar arrays in orbit to capture and transmit energy back to Earth.
Methods for transmitting energy from space-based solar panels to ground receiving stations.
Rubbish left over from past space missions that poses a risk of collision with operational satellites and spacecraft.

subsystems.name: Solar array
subsystems.role: collects sunlight uninterrupted by night or weather, at roughly several times the intensity available on the ground.
parts: lightweight thin-film or composite photovoltaic panels

subsystems.name: Power conversion and transmitter
subsystems.role: converts direct current into a microwave beam aimed at one spot on Earth.

subsystems.name: Beam steering and pilot link
subsystems.role: keeps the beam locked on the receiving site so energy lands only where intended.

subsystems.name: Structure and attitude control
subsystems.role: holds a structure kilometres across rigid enough to aim the beam precisely.
parts: thrusters and reaction wheels for station-keeping

subsystems.name: Rectenna
subsystems.role: the ground station: a field of antennas that turns microwaves back into electricity.

subsystems.name: Launch and orbital assembly
subsystems.role: gets thousands of tonnes of hardware into orbit and puts it together.

subsystems.name: Grid interface
subsystems.role: conditions the rectenna output for transmission to consumers.

buildSteps.title: Design for launch mass
buildSteps.detail: Every kilogram must be lifted to orbit, so panels, antennas and structure are engineered around minimum mass per watt rather than minimum cost.

buildSteps.title: Make the solar modules
buildSteps.detail: Thin-film or lightweight composite cells are laid onto flexible substrates that can be rolled up for launch.

buildSteps.title: Make the transmitting array
buildSteps.detail: Thousands of small solid-state amplifiers and antenna elements are built into flat tiles that can be joined edge to edge.

buildSteps.title: Launch the modules
buildSteps.detail: Reusable heavy-lift rockets carry tile stacks to a low parking orbit, a few hundred tonnes per station at a time.

buildSteps.title: Assemble in orbit
buildSteps.detail: Robotic arms or crews join modules into a flat array several kilometres across, then raise the orbit to geostationary altitude.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and test the beam
buildSteps.detail: The array unfolds, sun-tracking gimbals are commissioned, and the transmitter is phased against a pilot signal from the ground site.

buildSteps.title: Build the rectenna
buildSteps.detail: A field kilometres across is populated with antenna elements and rectifier circuits on land chosen for low population density.

buildSteps.title: Beam at low power
buildSteps.detail: Initial operation uses beam power densities well below sunlight intensity at the ground, to verify pointing and safety margins.

buildSteps.title: Scale to a pilot plant
buildSteps.detail: Power is stepped up and fed through inverters into the grid, while regulators confirm spectrum and exposure limits.

prerequisites.why: a single gigawatt station implies thousands of tonnes in orbit; today's launch prices make the electricity unaffordable.
kilowatts have been sent over tens of metres in ground tests, and a small in-orbit experiment (Caltech's SSPD-1, 2023) detected a faint signal on Earth, but nothing at power-plant scale.
kilometre-scale structures must be built automatically, which has only been done at much smaller scale.

prerequisites.tech: Lightweight high-efficiency photovoltaics and RF amplifiers
prerequisites.why: the physics works today, but efficiency and mass per watt must improve for the economics to close.
nobody has yet agreed international limits for a continuous microwave beam crossing airspace and inhabited land.

prerequisites.tech: Geostationary orbit capacity and debris rules
prerequisites.why: large fleets of very big satellites would need coordinated slots and end-of-life disposal.

pathway.milestone: sub-scale orbital and ground beaming demonstrations
pathway.unlocks: evidence that pointing, phasing and rectification work outside the laboratory.

pathway.milestone: a megawatt-class orbital demonstrator delivering measurable power to a grid-connected rectenna
pathway.unlocks: real cost and efficiency figures instead of estimates.

pathway.milestone: a pilot station of tens of megawatts with agreed spectrum and safety rules
pathway.unlocks: a credible comparison with terrestrial wind and solar.

pathway.milestone: gigawatt stations assembled from mass-produced modules
pathway.unlocks: firm, weather-independent power exported by beam to regions with poor renewable resources.
